meta_desc: A Class 2 logical reasoning worksheet guide: patterns, odd-one-out, analogies, coding and mirror images, plus a free quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: A seven-year-old who can add 8 and 5 can still freeze on ‘which one is different?’ Logical reasoning is a separate skill — here is exactly what a Class 2 logical reasoning worksheet trains, why it helps maths and olympiads, and a free quiz to try.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Show a Class 2 child four pictures — a rose, a lotus, a sunflower and a table — and ask which one does not belong. Plenty of seven-year-olds who can already add 8 and 5 will hesitate here. That pause is not a gap in maths; it is a gap in reasoning, and it is exactly what a good Class 2 logical reasoning worksheet is built to close. Reasoning is a separate muscle from arithmetic, and at this age it is far easier to grow than most parents expect.

I have watched bright children who race through number work stall on a simple pattern question, purely because nobody had ever asked them to look for the rule instead of the answer. So before you buy a stack of practice, it helps to know what ‘logical reasoning’ actually means for a seven-year-old — and what it does not.

What a Class 2 logical reasoning worksheet covers

At Class 2 level the questions stay concrete and visual. There is no algebra and no long reading. Instead a worksheet cycles through a small set of recognisable question types, each training a slightly different habit of thinking.

TypeWhat it trainsExample
Patterns & seriesSpotting the rule that repeats2, 4, 6, 8, ?
Odd one outSorting by a shared propertyCircle, ball, wheel, book
AnalogySeeing a relationship, then copying itHand : glove :: foot : ?
Mirror imagesLeft–right spatial senseMirror of the letter d
Coding–decodingFollowing a simple rule to swap symbolsA=1, B=2, so 3, 1, 2 = ?
Ranking & orderHolding a sequence in the headWho finished last in a race?

Notice how little arithmetic is involved. A child can be weak at times tables and still be excellent at odd-one-out — and the reverse is true too. That is the whole point: reasoning is its own skill.

The three types children find hardest

In my experience three types trip up Class 2 students most often. Mirror images are tough because a young child has not yet firmly separated b from d in their own mind. Analogies demand two steps — work out the link, then apply it — which is a genuine leap. And coding feels like a puzzle only until the child realises it is just a rule to follow, patiently, one letter at a time. Spend a little extra time on these three and the rest tend to follow.

Why reasoning quietly makes maths easier

Here is the counter-intuitive bit: reasoning practice improves maths marks even though the questions barely look like maths. Number patterns are the bridge. A child who can extend 5, 10, 15, 20 has, without being told, understood skip-counting and the seed of the multiplication table. Odd-one-out teaches classification, which is the same instinct a child later uses to tell even numbers from odd. Ranking questions build the ordered-number sense that place value depends on.

So the honest trade-off is this — ten minutes on reasoning is not ten minutes stolen from arithmetic. It is arithmetic wearing different clothes, and it keeps a child interested on the days plain sums feel like a chore.

Why it matters for olympiads

If your child sits any of the big Indian olympiads — the SOF International Maths Olympiad (IMO) or National Science Olympiad, or the Silverzone iOM — you will find a full section labelled ‘Logical Reasoning’ or ‘Mental Ability’ right at the start of the paper. It is not a bonus round. At the Class 2 level it can be a third of the marks, and it is often where the ranking is decided, because most children prepare only the maths half and walk in cold on the reasoning half.

That is genuinely good news for a parent. Reasoning is the most coachable part of an olympiad at this age — the question types repeat year after year, so a child who has seen twenty odd-one-out questions handles the twenty-first calmly. Steady exposure beats last-minute cramming every single time.

How to practise at home

You do not need an app or a tutor for this. A worksheet, a pencil and a short daily habit do more than an occasional long session. A routine I recommend to parents in Tier-2 cities, where a weekend coaching class is not always nearby:

  • Talk through the first one together. Ask ‘what is the rule?’ out loud before touching the pencil. Reasoning is a spoken skill first.
  • One type a day. Monday patterns, Tuesday odd-one-out, and so on. Mixing everything at once overwhelms a seven-year-old.
  • Let them be wrong, then ask why. The explanation matters more than the tick. A child who can say why the table does not belong with the flowers has actually learned something.
  • Save mixed sets for the weekend so the child has to choose which kind of thinking a question needs — that choosing step is where real ability shows.

One caveat worth stating plainly: do not push for speed yet. A child who reasons slowly but correctly at seven is in a far stronger position than one drilled to answer fast without understanding. Speed arrives on its own once the thinking is sound.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question reasoning quiz pitched exactly at Class 2 — patterns, odd-one-out, analogy, mirror images, coding and ranking, one of each kind. Let your child attempt it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Class 2 Logical Reasoning Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick reasoning questions covering patterns, odd-one-out, analogy, mirror images, coding and ranking. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 2 logical reasoning and mental ability

questions.q: Which one is the odd one out?
questions.explanation: A rose, a lotus and a sunflower are all flowers. A table is not, so it is the odd one out.

questions.q: What comes next in the pattern: 5, 10, 15, 20, ?
questions.explanation: The numbers go up by 5 each time. After 20 comes 25.

questions.q: Hand is to glove as foot is to ___?
questions.explanation: A glove covers the hand, so what covers the foot is a sock.

questions.q: Which letter is the mirror image of the letter d?
questions.explanation: Flipping d left-to-right in a mirror turns it into b.

questions.q: In a code, A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4. What word do the numbers 3, 1, 2 spell?
questions.explanation: 3 is C, 1 is A and 2 is B, so 3, 1, 2 spells CAB.

questions.q: Look at the pattern where each number doubles: 1, 2, 4, 8, ?
questions.explanation: Each number is doubled: 8 doubled is 16.

questions.q: In a line, Aarav stands ahead of Meera, and Meera stands ahead of Kabir. Who is last?
questions.explanation: The order is Aarav, then Meera, then Kabir. So Kabir is last.

questions.q: Which one does not belong with the others?
questions.explanation: A circle, a ball and a wheel are all round. A book is not round, so it does not belong.

faq.q: What is logical reasoning in Class 2?
faq.a: It is a set of visual thinking puzzles — patterns, odd-one-out, analogies, mirror images, simple coding and ranking — that train a child to spot rules and relationships rather than just calculate. There is no algebra or long reading at this level.

faq.q: Is logical reasoning different from maths?
faq.a: Yes. A child can be strong at reasoning but shaky at times tables, or the reverse. They are separate skills, though number patterns and skip-counting form a natural bridge between the two.

faq.q: Why is logical reasoning important for Class 2 olympiads?
faq.a: Papers like the SOF IMO and Silverzone iOM open with a Logical Reasoning or Mental Ability section that can be about a third of the marks. Most children prepare only the maths half, so reasoning is often where ranks are won or lost.

faq.q: How can I help my child practise reasoning at home?
faq.a: Do one question type a day, talk through the rule out loud before writing, and always ask why an answer is right or wrong. Keep mixed sets for the weekend, and do not push for speed — correct-but-slow beats fast-but-confused at this age.
